Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis. It causes dark, scabby lesions on leaves and fruit.
Apple___Apple_scab.dosage: Captan: 2.5 g/L water | Mancozeb: 2 g/L water | Myclobutanil: 0.5 g/L water
Apple___Apple_scab.application_method: Spray evenly on all leaf surfaces and fruit. Apply every 7–10 days during wet weather. Begin at bud break and continue through petal fall.
precautions: Wear protective gloves and mask when handling chemicals
Do not spray during rain or when wind speed is high
Avoid spraying near water bodies
Observe a pre-harvest interval of 14 days
Remove and destroy infected leaves to reduce spore load
Apple___Apple_scab.cultural_practices: Prune trees for better air circulation. Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn. Plant resistant varieties.

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is a fungal disease caused by Botryosphaeria obtusa, causing circular lesions on leaves, fruit rot, and cankers on branches.
Apple___Black_rot.dosage: Thiophanate-methyl: 1 g/L | Captan: 2.5 g/L | Ziram: 3 mL/L water
Apple___Black_rot.application_method: Start applications at pink stage and continue through cover sprays. Spray every 10–14 days. Ensure thorough coverage of fruit and foliage.
precautions: Prune and remove dead branches to eliminate overwintering sites
Protect spray equipment from cross-contamination
Use fungicides in rotation to prevent resistance
Apple___Black_rot.cultural_practices: Remove mummified fruits. Prune infected branches well below canker margins. Improve drainage.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar-apple rust is caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae, creating orange, gall-like lesions on leaves.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.dosage: Myclobutanil: 0.5 g/L | Propiconazole: 1 mL/L | Mancozeb: 2 g/L water
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.application_method: Apply at pink bud stage through late petal fall. Spray every 7–10 days during humid weather. Target all leaf surfaces.
precautions: Avoid planting apple trees near eastern red cedar or juniper trees
Use personal protective equipment when spraying
Alternate fungicide classes to prevent resistance development
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cultural_practices: Remove nearby cedar/juniper galls if possible. Plant rust-resistant apple varieties.

Apple___healthy.description: The apple plant appears healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
Apple___healthy.application_method: Maintain regular preventive spray schedule during high-risk periods.
precautions: Continue regular monitoring
Maintain good orchard hygiene
Apple___healthy.cultural_practices: Regular pruning, proper fertilization, and balanced irrigation.

Blueberry___healthy.description: The blueberry plant is healthy with no signs of disease.
precautions: Monitor for pests and diseases regularly
Blueberry___healthy.cultural_practices: Maintain soil pH between 4.5–5.5. Mulch around base.

Cherry___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cherry is caused by Podosphaera clandestina, creating white powdery growth on leaves and young shoots.
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.dosage: Sulfur: 3 g/L | Trifloxystrobin: 0.3 g/L | Potassium bicarbonate: 5 g/L water
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.application_method: Begin applications at first sign of infection. Spray every 10–14 days. Ensure thorough coverage of new growth. Avoid spraying in high temperatures (>32°C).
precautions: Do not apply sulfur in hot weather — risk of phytotoxicity
Rotate fungicide classes each spray
Wear protective clothing when handling sulfur products
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.cultural_practices: Prune for open canopy. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilization. Plant resistant varieties.

Cherry___healthy.description: The cherry plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
precautions: Monitor regularly for early signs of powdery mildew

Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot.description: Gray leaf spot caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis produces rectangular, gray to tan lesions on corn leaves.
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot.dosage: Azoxystrobin: 1 mL/L | Propiconazole: 1 mL/L | Pyraclostrobin: 0.8 mL/L water
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot.application_method: Apply at VT/R1 growth stage (tasseling/silking). Use thorough canopy-penetrating spray. Repeat in 14–21 days if disease pressure remains high.
precautions: Rotate fungicide classes each season
Avoid applications during extreme heat
Check resistance management guidelines for strobilurins
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot.cultural_practices: Rotate crops with non-host plants. Use resistant hybrids. Tillage to reduce leaf residue.

Corn___Common_rust.description: Common rust (Puccinia sorghi) causes small, circular to elongated, brick-red pustules on corn leaf surfaces.
Corn___Common_rust.dosage: Quilt Xcel: 1.5 mL/L | Stratego: 0.5 mL/L | Mancozeb: 2 g/L water
Corn___Common_rust.application_method: Spray at first sign of rust pustules. Apply at VT to R2 growth stage. Ensure good coverage of upper and lower leaf surfaces.
precautions: Avoid repeated use of single-mode-of-action fungicides
Store fungicides away from feed and seeds
Wear gloves and eye protection during mixing
Corn___Common_rust.cultural_practices: Plant resistant hybrids. Scout regularly from V6 stage. Adequate plant spacing for airflow.

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight (Exserohilum turcicum) causes large, tan, cigar-shaped lesions on corn leaves, starting from lower leaves.
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.dosage: Azoxystrobin: 1 mL/L | Propiconazole: 1 mL/L | Prothioconazole: 0.6 mL/L water
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.application_method: Apply at tasseling when first lesions appear. Repeat at 14-day intervals under severe conditions. Target full canopy coverage.
precautions: Observe pre-harvest intervals strictly
Rotate with non-maize crops in heavily infected fields
Do not mix incompatible chemicals
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.cultural_practices: Use resistant hybrids. Crop rotation. Tillage to break down infected residue.

Corn___healthy.description: The corn plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
precautions: Scout regularly from V6 onwards
Corn___healthy.cultural_practices: Maintain balanced nitrogen. Optimal population density.

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot (Guignardia bidwellii) causes brown lesions on leaves with black pycnidia and mummified fruits.
Grape___Black_rot.dosage: Mancozeb: 2 g/L | Myclobutanil: 0.5 g/L | Captan: 2.5 g/L water
Grape___Black_rot.application_method: Begin at bud break, spray every 10–14 days through veraison. Apply before and after rain events. Thorough coverage of all shoot and fruit surfaces.
precautions: Remove mummified berries and infected canes before new season
Avoid working in vineyard when leaves are wet
Pre-harvest interval: 14 days for most fungicides
Grape___Black_rot.cultural_practices: Prune for open canopy. Remove mummified fruits. Shoot positioning for airflow.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca is a complex wood disease of grapevines causing interveinal leaf scorch, berry spotting, and internal wood decay.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).dosage: Thiophanate-methyl paint: apply undiluted to pruning wounds | Trichoderma: follow label
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).application_method: Protect all pruning wounds immediately after cutting. Apply wound protectant paste or spray within 24 hours. Biological agents can be applied to soil around root zone.
precautions: There is no cure once wood is infected — focus on prevention
Disinfect pruning tools between vines with 70% alcohol
Remove and burn severely infected vines
Avoid large pruning wounds by training young vines carefully
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).cultural_practices: Prune during dry weather. Double pruning technique to delay trunk exposure. Replace infected vines.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Leaf blight (Isariopsis clavispora) causes dark brown lesions with yellow halos on older grape leaves.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.dosage: Copper hydroxide: 2.5 g/L | Mancozeb: 2 g/L | Ridomil Gold MZ: 2.5 g/L water
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.application_method: Spray at first sign of disease. Apply every 10–14 days in humid weather. Focus especially on older foliage where infection begins.
precautions: Avoid excess copper accumulation in soil
Wear PPI during copper sprays
Rotate active ingredients to manage resistance
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.cultural_practices: Remove infected leaves. Improve canopy ventilation. Avoid overhead irrigation.

Grape___healthy.description: The grape plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
precautions: Regular scouting essential in humid climates

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB) or citrus greening is a severe bacterial disease spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, causing blotchy yellowing, small misshapen fruit, and eventual tree death.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).dosage: Imidacloprid soil drench: 0.5 g/L per tree | Oxytetracycline: follow certified applicator dosing
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).application_method: There is NO cure for HLB. Management focuses on: (1) Controlling the Asian citrus psyllid vector with insecticides every 3 weeks during new flush. (2) Removing and destroying infected trees. (3) Antibiotic injections may temporarily improve tree appearance but do not cure the disease.
precautions: Remove and destroy all infected trees immediately to prevent spread
Do not move plant material out of infected areas
Antibiotic trunk injections require licensed professional applicators
Report suspected HLB to local agricultural authorities immediately
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cultural_practices: Plant certified disease-free nursery stock. Use reflective mulch to repel psyllids. Quarantine measures.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot (Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni) causes water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark and fall out, leaving shot-holes.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.dosage: Copper hydroxide: 2–3 g/L | Oxytetracycline: 1 g/L | Bordeaux 1%: 10 g copper sulfate + 10 g lime per liter
Peach___Bacterial_spot.application_method: Begin copper applications at dormancy/delayed-dormancy. Apply oxytetracycline at shuck split through cover sprays every 7–10 days. Stop copper by shuck split to avoid phytotoxicity.
precautions: Do not apply copper during green tip or after petal fall if phytotoxicity risk is high
Oxytetracycline resistance can develop — rotate with copper products
Plant on well-drained sites with good air circulation
Peach___Bacterial_spot.cultural_practices: Plant resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation. Prune infected shoots.

Peach___healthy.description: The peach plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
Peach___healthy.application_method: Continue preventive copper program during dormancy.
precautions: Scout for bacterial spot in wet seasons

Pepper_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot (Xanthomonas spp.) causes water-soaked lesions on pepper leaves and fruit that turn dark brown with yellow halos.
Pepper_bell___Bacterial_spot.dosage: Copper hydroxide: 2.5 g/L | Badge X2: 2 g/L | Actigard: 0.05 g/L water
Pepper_bell___Bacterial_spot.application_method: Begin applications when seedlings are transplanted. Apply every 5–7 days in wet/warm conditions. Alternate copper with Actigard sprays for resistance management.
precautions: Use pathogen-free certified seed
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip irrigation where possible
Limit copper use to avoid fruit russeting
Do not save seed from infected plants
Pepper_bell___Bacterial_spot.cultural_practices: 3-year crop rotation. Weed control. Sanitize equipment between fields.

Pepper_bell___healthy.description: The bell pepper plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
Pepper_bell___healthy.application_method: Maintain preventive spray schedule during wet weather.
precautions: Use certified disease-free transplants

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight (Alternaria solani) causes dark brown concentric-ring lesions on older potato leaves, leading to premature defoliation.
Potato___Early_blight.dosage: Chlorothalonil: 2 mL/L | Azoxystrobin: 0.8 mL/L | Mancozeb: 2 g/L water
Potato___Early_blight.application_method: Begin applications at canopy closure or when first symptoms appear. Spray every 7–10 days. Ensure full coverage of both leaf surfaces. Stop 7–14 days before harvest.
precautions: Rotate fungicides — alternate strobilurins with protectants
Avoid applying in hot midday sun
Maintain good nutrition especially adequate potassium
Potato___Early_blight.cultural_practices: Use certified seed potatoes. Avoid overhead irrigation. Destroy crop debris after harvest.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) is one of the most destructive potato diseases, causing water-soaked dark lesions that spread rapidly in cool, wet weather.
Potato___Late_blight.dosage: Ridomil Gold MZ: 2.5 g/L | Curzate M8: 2 g/L | Acrobat MZ: 2 g/L water
Potato___Late_blight.application_method: Begin preventive sprays at tuber initiation or at first blight alert. Apply every 5–7 days during wet conditions. Rotate between fungicide groups. Apply with high volume to ensure canopy saturation.
precautions: CRITICAL: Act immediately — late blight can destroy a field in days
Metalaxyl resistance is widespread — always mix with a protectant fungicide
Destroy infected plant material — do not compost
Observe pre-harvest intervals strictly
Haulm desiccation 2–3 weeks before harvest to protect tubers
Potato___Late_blight.cultural_practices: Use resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation. Good hilling to protect tubers.

Potato___healthy.description: The potato plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
Potato___healthy.application_method: Continue preventive blight spray program during high-risk periods.
precautions: Monitor daily during cool, wet weather

Raspberry___healthy.description: The raspberry plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
Raspberry___healthy.application_method: Maintain regular scouting and preventive care.
precautions: Watch for cane diseases after harvest
Raspberry___healthy.cultural_practices: Proper pruning and good air circulation.

Soybean___healthy.description: The soybean plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
precautions: Monitor for sudden death syndrome and soybean rust
Soybean___healthy.cultural_practices: Crop rotation and proper seeding rates.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew (Podosphaera xanthii) forms white powdery patches on squash leaves, reducing photosynthesis and yield.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.dosage: Sulfur: 3 g/L | Potassium bicarbonate: 5 g/L | Azoxystrobin: 0.8 mL/L water
Squash___Powdery_mildew.application_method: Spray at first sign of white powdery patches. Apply every 7–10 days. Focus on upper and lower leaf surfaces. Avoid applying sulfur in temperatures above 32°C.
precautions: Do not apply sulfur within 2 weeks of oil-based pesticides
Rotate fungicide classes
Wear eye protection with sulfur dust applications
Squash___Powdery_mildew.cultural_practices: Increase plant spacing. Avoid overhead irrigation. Use resistant varieties.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch (Diplocarpon earlianum) causes small, dark purple to reddish spots on strawberry leaves that expand and cause leaf death.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.dosage: Captan: 2.5 g/L | Myclobutanil: 0.5 g/L | Thiram: 2 g/L water
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.application_method: Apply at first sign of disease. Spray every 7–10 days during spring and fall when infection is common. After renovation (mowing), apply a protective fungicide.
precautions: Do not apply Thiram within 3 days of harvest
Observe all pre-harvest intervals strictly
Wear protective gloves when handling Thiram
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.cultural_practices: Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves. Use drip irrigation. Rotate planting beds every 2 years.

Strawberry___healthy.description: The strawberry plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
Strawberry___healthy.application_method: Preventive fungicide sprays after renovation mowing.
precautions: Monitor for leaf scorch during wet spring weather

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot (Xanthomonas spp.) causes water-soaked spots on tomato leaves and fruit that turn dark, scabby, and sunken.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.dosage: Copper hydroxide: 2.5 g/L | Cueva: 5 mL/L | Actigard: 0.05 g/L water
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.application_method: Apply at transplanting. Spray every 5–7 days in hot, wet weather. Rotate copper with Actigard every other spray. Ensure thorough coverage — spray early morning to allow foliage to dry.
precautions: Use certified disease-free transplants — crucial for prevention
Avoid working in field when foliage is wet
Do not save seed from infected fruits
Sanitize stakes and cages with 10% bleach solution between seasons
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cultural_practices: 2-3 year crop rotation. Drip irrigation. Proper staking for airflow.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight (Alternaria solani) causes dark concentric-ring lesions starting on older tomato leaves, moving upward as the season progresses.
Tomato___Early_blight.dosage: Chlorothalonil: 2 mL/L | Amistar Top: 1 mL/L | Mancozeb: 2 g/L water
Tomato___Early_blight.application_method: Start at first sign of disease or at transplanting in wet conditions. Spray every 7–10 days. Target lower leaves first, work upward. Remove heavily infected lower leaves before spraying.
precautions: Rotate fungicide classes to prevent resistance
Allow 7-14 day pre-harvest interval
Do not spray in high temperatures during midday
Tomato___Early_blight.cultural_practices: Remove infected lower leaves. Dense mulch to reduce soil splash. Proper stakes and ties.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) in tomatoes causes rapidly spreading water-soaked lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit, with white sporulation in humid conditions.
Tomato___Late_blight.dosage: Ridomil Gold MZ: 2.5 g/L | Curzate M8: 2 g/L | Chlorothalonil: 2 mL/L water
Tomato___Late_blight.application_method: Begin preventive sprays at first blight risk or when first symptoms appear. Apply every 5–7 days during wet weather. Spray under and over leaf surfaces. Act immediately — late blight spreads very rapidly.
precautions: URGENT: Destroy infected plants immediately to prevent spread
Never compost infected plant material
Do not work in field when foliage is wet
Rotate fungicide groups strictly — Metalaxyl resistance is common
Observe all pre-harvest intervals
Tomato___Late_blight.cultural_practices: Destroy volunteer potato plants nearby. Avoid overhead irrigation. Stake plants well.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Leaf mold (Passalora fulva) causes pale yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces and olive-green to grayish-brown velvety mold on undersides.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.dosage: Chlorothalonil: 2 mL/L | Mancozeb: 2 g/L | Azoxystrobin: 0.8 mL/L water
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.application_method: This disease is primarily a greenhouse problem. Improve ventilation before chemical treatment. Apply sprays to lower leaf surfaces where sporulation occurs. Spray every 7–10 days.
precautions: Critical: Reduce relative humidity below 85% inside greenhouses — this is the primary control
Remove infected leaves and destroy them
Avoid wetting foliage with overhead irrigation
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cultural_practices: Improve greenhouse ventilation. Reduce humidity. Use resistant varieties (Cf gene resistance).

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot (Septoria lycopersici) causes numerous small circular spots with dark borders and tan/white centers on lower tomato leaves.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.dosage: Chlorothalonil: 2 mL/L | Mancozeb: 2 g/L | Amistar Top: 1 mL/L water
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.application_method: Begin sprays when first spots appear on lower leaves. Apply every 7–10 days. Remove infected lower leaves before spraying. Target undersides of leaves where spores are produced.
precautions: Do not compost infected plant debris
Rotate fungicide classes each spray
Avoid working in wet tomato plantings
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cultural_practices: Mulch to prevent soil splash. Stake plants. Multi-year crop rotation (3+ years).

Tomato___Spider_mites.description: Two-spotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae) cause stippling and bronzing on tomato leaves, with fine webbing visible on undersides in severe cases.
Tomato___Spider_mites.dosage: Abamectin: 0.5 mL/L | Bifenazate: 1 mL/L | Spiromesifen: 0.75 mL/L water
Tomato___Spider_mites.application_method: Spray both upper and lower leaf surfaces — spider mites feed on undersides. Apply in early morning or evening. A second application 5–7 days later is critical to break the mite life cycle.
precautions: Rotate acaricide classes — mite resistance develops quickly
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural predators
Do not apply in temperatures above 35°C
Tomato___Spider_mites.cultural_practices: Maintain well-irrigated plants — drought stresses plants and worsens mite damage. Introduce predatory mites (Phytoseiidae) in IPM programs.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot (Corynespora cassiicola) causes dark brown, concentric-ring lesions on tomato leaves, stems, and fruit.
Tomato___Target_Spot.dosage: Azoxystrobin: 0.8 mL/L | Pristine: 0.5 g/L | Chlorothalonil: 2 mL/L water
Tomato___Target_Spot.application_method: Apply at first sign of disease. Spray every 7–14 days. Ensure thorough coverage of all plant surfaces including stems. Remove heavily infected leaves before spraying.
precautions: Rotate between SDHI, strobilurin, and contact fungicides
Pre-harvest interval: 7 days for azoxystrobin
Do not overuse strobilurins — resistance risk
Tomato___Target_Spot.cultural_practices: Improve air circulation through training and pruning. Mulch to prevent spore splash.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: TYLCV is a highly destructive begomovirus transmitted by whiteflies. It causes upward leaf curling, yellowing, stunting, and severe yield loss.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.dosage: Imidacloprid: 0.5 mL/L | Thiamethoxam: 0.2 g/L | Pymetrozine: 0.5 g/L water
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.application_method: PREVENTION IS CRITICAL — there is no cure once plants are infected. Control whitefly vector with systemic insecticides applied to soil at transplanting (drench) + foliar sprays every 7–10 days. Use yellow sticky traps for monitoring.
precautions: Remove and destroy infected plants to reduce inoculum
Rotate insecticide classes strictly — whitefly resistance is a major problem
Avoid planting near older tomato or other host crops
Use reflective mulch to deter whiteflies
Screen greenhouse vents with insect-proof mesh
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cultural_practices: Plant TYLCV-resistant varieties (strong protection). Rogue infected plants early. Use certified whitefly-free transplants.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) causes light and dark green mottling on leaves, distortion, and stunting. It is mechanically transmitted through contact.

medicines.name: Antiviral agents are not commercially viable

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.application_method: PREVENTION AND SANITATION are the ONLY effective controls. Roguing (removing infected plants) is the primary action.
precautions: IMMEDIATELY remove and destroy infected plants — do not compost
CRITICAL: workers must wash hands and disinfect tools (10% bleach or 70% alcohol) between plants
Do not smoke near tomato crops — tobacco can carry ToMV
Do not use infected seed
Avoid touching healthy plants after handling infected ones
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cultural_practices: Use certified virus-free seed (seed can be heat treated at 70°C for 3 days). Plant resistant varieties (Tm-2² gene). Strict sanitation protocols.

Tomato___healthy.description: The tomato plant is healthy with no visible disease symptoms.
precautions: Regular scouting essential — tomato is susceptible to many diseases
Tomato___healthy.cultural_practices: Balanced fertilization, consistent irrigation, staking for airflow.
